description:
The term '''bard''' ({{lang|ru|бард}}) came to be used in the [[Soviet Union]] in the early 1960s, and continues to be used in Russia and some other [[post-Soviet states]] today, to refer to [[singer-songwriter]]s who wrote and performed songs outside the Soviet establishment. Because in bard music songwriters perform their own songs, the genre is also commonly referred to as '''author song''' ({{langx|ru|авторская песня}}, ''avtorskaya pesnya'') or '''bard song''' ({{langx|ru|бардовская песня}}, ''bardovskaya pesnya'').

Stylistically, the precursors to bard songs were Russian {{ill|lt=urban romances|urban romance|ru|Городской романс}}, which touched upon common life and were popular throughout all layers of Russian society in the late 19th to early 20th centuries. These romances were traditionally written in a minor key and performed with a guitar accompaniment.

Bard poetry may be roughly classified into two main genres: ''tourist song'' and ''political song'', although some other subgenres are also recognized, such as ''outlaw song'' and ''pirate song''.

Initially the term "bard" was used by fans of the tourist song genre, and outside those circles, the term was often perceived as slightly derisive. However, there was a need for a term to distinguish this style of song from the traditional mainstream pop song, and the term eventually stuck.

In the 1950s and 1960s, author's songs circulated through informal networks of students, friends and amateur performers. They were sung at gatherings, including performances in private apartments, but the movement was not confined to domestic settings. Clubs of Amateur Song (''kluby samodeyatel'noy pesni'', or KSP) and other organized venues also became important: regular song evenings were held at Leningrad's Vostok café from 1963, a city song club opened there in 1965, and a Moscow KSP was established in 1966.

The growing availability of reel-to-reel tape recorders enabled songs to circulate beyond the audiences who had heard them performed. Recordings were copied and passed between listeners, a practice associated with ''[[magnitizdat]]''. This was particularly important for performers whose access to official recording and concert institutions was limited, although the circumstances varied among artists and over time. Musicologist J. Martin Daughtry examines unofficial recordings of [[author's song]], including a likely private house performance by [[Alexander Galich (writer)|Alexander Galich]], and shows how the recordings preserved not only the songs but also traces of their performance settings. The domestic concert tradition is also associated with the ''[[kvartirnik]]'', a form of informal gathering in a private apartment.
